summary:
Finland presents very low legal and physical risk to trans visitors. There is no criminalisation of gender identity or expression, no documented case of tourist-targeted sexual violence, mob violence or police brutality against a trans person in the country, and no reported restriction on trans access to public facilities such as bathrooms and changing rooms. The Schengen border applies no trans-specific screening, and no source reports entry-document friction for trans travellers arriving in Finland.

Hate-crime recording is the principal quantified indicator of the ambient risk environment. The Police University College (Polamk) recorded 1,808 suspected hate-crime offenses, the highest figure ever logged, with defamation and assault the most common types. The category covering sexual orientation and gender identity or expression climbed across the six reported years, from 72 to 68, 126, 140, 215 and finally 241. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2026 records 1,808 suspected hate crimes in 2025, a 13% rise since 2023, with sexual orientation and gender identity recurrent motives in 12% of cases. No source breaks these figures down by victim status, so none of them measures incidents involving trans visitors.

The Finnish Criminal Code contains no hate-crime offence. Motive is captured only in police reports, which means sexual-orientation and gender-identity-motivated incidents are counted as reported suspicion rather than as charges. For a visitor, the practical consequence is that police recording of motive is available, but the statistics say nothing about prosecution or conviction outcomes.

Conversion practices have drawn official action but are not yet banned outright. Finland's first conversion-practices case was prosecuted as assault, with convictions in March 2025, and Parliament endorsed a citizens' initiative to prohibit conversion practices by 125 votes to 49 the same month. A full statutory ban remained pending at the time of the review.

On legal gender recognition, Finland explicitly wrote an infertility requirement into law. That requirement was phased out at the end of June 2025, placing Finland's statutory sterilisation era behind it, although the legacy cohort is documented. Across the six countries investigated in the same study, at least 11,000 people were subjected to such conditions, with Sweden the first to legislate them in 1972 and keep them in force for 40 years. No source in this inventory describes the current statutory test for changing a gender marker, and none reports document screening of trans travellers at the Finnish border.

Partner recognition is settled law. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption became legal in Finland on 1 March 2017, and Parliament approved a Maternity Act change on 28 February 2018 that recognises both women in a same-sex partnership as mothers from the moment of birth, fixing second-parent registration at birth rather than through adoption.
tangentialFactors:
Finland has treated trans document problems at foreign borders as an outbound-travel matter rather than a domestic one. In March 2025 Finland and Denmark updated their travel advice for transgender citizens travelling to the United States following reports of border difficulties after the US 'two genders' executive order, with Denmark advising trans travellers to contact the US embassy in Copenhagen before departure over document issues. That guidance concerns risk to Finnish travellers elsewhere and makes no assessment of conditions within Finland.

Finland's sterilisation-era gender-recognition rule sits within a wider northern European pattern. The Netherlands and Sweden wrote the same infertility requirement into law alongside Finland; Sweden legislated earliest, in 1972, and kept the condition in force for four decades. At least 11,000 people were subjected to such conditions across the six countries examined.

Marriage equality arrived through mass civic mobilisation rather than litigation. The 'Tahdon2013' citizens' initiative collected more than 162,000 certified signatures, the largest Finnish initiative ever and far above the 50,000 threshold that compels parliamentary consideration, against an organiser target of 250,000. Uptake after the 2017 law was immediate: the western Finland register office alone had about 41 same-sex couples scheduled to marry in the first week.
localsOnly:
Residents seeking to change legal gender no longer face the statutory infertility requirement, which ceased to apply at the end of June 2025. A documented cohort of people remains affected by the earlier condition, and the sources do not set out the replacement procedure.

Anyone reporting a motivated attack interacts with a police recording system rather than a distinct criminal charge. Police document motive, including sexual orientation and gender identity or expression, in the report, but the Criminal Code offers no hate-crime category under which to charge it. Defamation and assault are the offence types most often recorded alongside motive.

Conversion practices remain legally unconstrained by a general statute. Prosecutors pursued the country's first such case as assault and secured convictions in March 2025, and Parliament backed a citizens' initiative to ban the practice by 125 to 49 in the same month, but the comprehensive prohibition was still pending.

Family law provisions are established. Marriage and joint adoption have been available since 1 March 2017, and since 28 February 2018 both women in a same-sex partnership are named as the child's mothers from birth without a second-parent adoption.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 1,808 suspected hate-crime total is dated differently across sources: the Police University College attributes it to 2024 in a November 2025 release, while ILGA-Europe attributes the same figure to 2025. The discrepancy is unresolved.

Whether the police category combines sexual orientation with gender identity or counts them separately is not stated, and ILGA-Europe's 12% figure carries no trans-only breakdown. Prosecution and conviction rates for motive-recorded incidents are not sourced.

No source in this inventory records an incident involving a trans visitor to Finland, and the absence of such a record is not evidence that none occurs. The inventory also contains nothing on the legal status of bathroom and changing-room access, on healthcare access for trans visitors, or on document screening at Finnish border points; the facility and border statements in the summary rest on the standing profile rather than on a source here.

Whether the conversion-practices ban endorsed in March has since been enacted, and what the current statutory test for legal gender recognition now requires, remain unresolved.
